# Draft:Mwanza Ward:Goromonzi

----
Mwanza is a communal ward in Goromonzi District, Mashonaland East Province, Zimbabwe, designated Ward 12 of the district. It forms part of the Chikwaka Communal Lands and falls within the Goromonzi North parliamentary constituency. The 2022 National Census recorded a ward population of 18,178, up from 14,543 in 2012. The ward falls under the traditional jurisdiction of the Chikwaka Chieftaincy, whose ruling lineage — the Benhura Murambiwa dynasty of the Nzou, Mbano Matemavi (Elephant) totem — has held authority over the surrounding communal lands since the pre-colonial period.
Geography
Mwanza ward is situated within the Chikwaka Communal Lands in northern Goromonzi District, which covers approximately 9,100 square kilometres in Mashonaland East Province. The district lies east of Harare; Mwanza ward occupies the Goromonzi North zone, a predominantly communal farming area. The landscape is typical Highveld, with deep alluvial soils, an elevation of roughly 1,345 metres above sea level, and seasonal rainfall patterns suited to arable agriculture — though the area consistently produces below its agricultural potential.
The 2024 Goromonzi RDC Master Plan classifies Mwanza as part of the Juru-Mwanza Corridor and designates it among the district's unplanned, fast-urbanising nodes, under pressure from in-migration and informal settlement expansion. The 2000 Goromonzi RDC Operative Master Plan had earlier proposed a satellite administrative centre at Mwanza — alongside Bosha and Rusike — as a decentralised service-delivery node.
Administration
Mwanza is Ward 12 of Goromonzi District, administered by the Goromonzi Rural District Council and represented in the House of Assembly through the Goromonzi North constituency. Ward boundaries were last revised under the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission's 2023 Delimitation Report.
Under Zimbabwe's Traditional Leaders Act [Chapter 29:17], the ward falls within the jurisdiction of Chief Chikwaka. The current and eleventh Chief Chikwaka, Murambiwa Witness Bungu, was appointed on 1 February 2013. His installation has been subject to community dispute: in 2022, villagers petitioned the Ministry of Local Government citing procedural irregularities in the appointment, and a spirit medium (svikiro) associated with the ancestral spirit Benhura was reported to have become involved in the dispute.
The ward-level headmanship, Headman Mwanza, is held by Mr Clemence Chihuri of the Gurundebvu/Chihuri family line. In February 2023, Headman Chihuri publicly endorsed the commissioning of staff buses by Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe, describing it as "a safer way of travelling" and a community benefit.
In July 2025, Chief Chikwaka and Headman Musonza wrote to state authorities over the acquisition of ancestral land in Ward 16 of Goromonzi District by the Air Force of Zimbabwe, stating the land had been held by the community "for generations and generations."
History
Pre-colonial period
The land comprising present-day Mwanza ward has been settled since at least the early second millennium as part of the broader territory of the Shona-speaking peoples of northern Mashonaland. Oral traditions recorded by the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation in 2023 place the origins of the Chikwaka chieftaincy and its associated communities — including those in the Mwanza area — within the pre-Rozvi Shona polities of Mashonaland.
Colonial period
Under British South Africa Company and subsequent Southern Rhodesia administration, the Mwanza and Chikwaka area was designated as a Tribal Trust Land (TTL) under the Land Apportionment Act of 1930 and the Land Tenure Act of 1969. Colonial records in the National Archives of Zimbabwe's S.401 series document administration of the Chikwaka chieftaincy during this period, including succession proceedings and management of the communal lands. Members of the Benhura Murambiwa dynasty are recorded in oral tradition as participants in the First Chimurenga (1896–1897).
Post-independence
Following independence in 1980, Tribal Trust Lands became Communal Lands under the Communal Land Act [Chapter 20:04], with the Chikwaka Communal Lands — including Mwanza ward — placed under the Goromonzi Rural District Council and the restored Chikwaka chieftaincy. From 2000, the Fast Track Land Reform Programme dismantled the commercial farming sector that had previously provided significant employment in Goromonzi District, increasing dependence on subsistence agriculture across communal wards including Mwanza.
Health
The primary health facility for Mwanza ward is the Mwanza Rural Health Centre, a government clinic within the Chikwaka Communal Lands and one of only seven government-owned health facilities among the district's 29 total.
On 27 September 2012, the clinic served as the launch venue for the Gender Challenge Initiative (GCI), a PEPFAR-funded programme implemented by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in partnership with Zimbabwe's Ministry of Health to address gender inequalities driving HIV/AIDS transmission.
A Community Working Group on Health (CWGH) has operated a Health Centre Committee at the facility for over a decade. Following community health worker mobilisation, patient attendance grew from around 350 patients per month to between 500 and 650, and monthly deliveries rose from an average of 15 to approximately 24. A waiting mothers' home was established as a community initiative for pregnant women from outlying villages. Coverage by village health workers remains limited; one health report noted a single VHW serving five surrounding villages.
Education
Ward 12 has four registered primary schools and two registered secondary schools as of 2021, according to the 2024 Goromonzi RDC Master Plan.
Mwanza Primary School is a government primary school. In 2023, Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe (PLZ) erected a perimeter fence at the school and provided new furniture and textbooks as part of a broader US$2.5 million corporate social responsibility programme across Goromonzi District.
Mwanza High School is a government secondary school at Juru, Goromonzi (P.O. Box 160), headed by Mr Maviva and deputised by Ms Chiketa. In 2023, PLZ refurbished the school's science laboratory and supplied A-Level textbooks in preparation for the launch of Advanced Level classes — one of only 12 schools in the district approved for A-Level examinations. On 23 May 2024, the school hosted the PLZ Africa Day celebration themed Light of Africa, Exploring Cultural Heritage, organised in partnership with the Confucius Institute and the Chinese Chamber of Commerce.
Economy
Mwanza ward's economy is predominantly subsistence-based. Goromonzi District recorded an average poverty prevalence of 62.4% in the 2015 Zimbabwe Poverty Atlas, with communal wards recording the highest rates in the district. Documented livelihood activities in Ward 12 include maricho (casual agricultural labour), vending of vegetables and dairy products, maize and tobacco farming, market gardening, and small-scale poultry rearing.
Smallholder dairy farming is practised in the Chikwaka Communal Lands. A peer-reviewed study by the University of Liverpool's Faculty of Veterinary Science found calf mortality of 35% within the first year on farms in the area, identifying Jersey crossbreeding as a risk factor.
Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe (PLZ), a subsidiary of Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, operates a US$300 million lithium processing plant in Goromonzi District, commissioned by President Emmerson Mnangagwa in 2023. The plant employs more than 1,200 people and PLZ has invested over US$2.5 million in community programmes across 13 wards, including Mwanza.
Infrastructure and transport
Two named roads serve Mwanza ward, as recorded in the 2024 Goromonzi RDC Master Plan:
* Mwanza – Chinyika Farm Road (Road ID 104): 4 km, high-traffic classification, 5 culverts.
* Mwanza – Loop Road (Road ID 311): 5 km, low-traffic classification, 7 culverts and 2 bridge structures.
The ward connects to the wider district via the Juru – Chiparambe – Dzvete Road (Road ID C31-105, 29 km). The 2024 Master Plan notes that the district's 1,700 km road network is largely in poor condition, with communal ward roads most affected.
In February 2023, PLZ commissioned staff buses to serve its workforce, many of whom commute from Mwanza and Harare. The commissioning ceremony was attended by Chief Chikwaka and Headman Mwanza.
Land and environment
Mwanza ward faces increasing pressure from urban encroachment linked to Harare's expanding metropolitan area. Since the 1990s, conflicts between residents and the Goromonzi RDC over peri-urban land have grown, with households selling land under financial duress. In 2025, communities in the Chikwaka Communal Lands raised formal objections over state land acquisitions, including by the Air Force of Zimbabwe in Ward 16.
The 2000 Operative Master Plan designated a zone of scenic beauty that included Mwanza Estate among several farms. Most were redistributed under A1 and A2 resettlement schemes from 2000 onwards. The Kunzwi Dam Project, a major water infrastructure initiative in Goromonzi District, is expected to provide a permanent water source for the greater Harare region and bring secondary economic opportunities to surrounding communities.
